headline: Lenovo's first Googlebooks have leaked, revealing two laptops and a 2-in-1 tablet
summary: Leaked images show two laptop models and a tablet, all featuring a distinctive "Glowbar" light strip, hinting at Google's new AI-powered platform.
details: Leaked images reveal Lenovo is preparing at least three devices for Google's new 'Googlebooks' initiative. The lineup includes two laptop sizes, similar to Lenovo's Chromebook Plus 14, and a 2-in-1 tablet resembling the IdeaPad Pro Gen 2. This marks the first concrete look at the hardware for Google's Android-based ChromeOS platform.

All three devices sport a stark white design and feature a 'Glowbar' light strip, a mysterious new hardware element Google intends to differentiate Googlebooks. This glowing light feature is also expected in upcoming Pixel phones, suggesting a cohesive design language.

The inclusion of a 2-in-1 tablet expands the Googlebook vision beyond laptops, as Google's initial announcement only showcased an unknown laptop. This indicates the AI-powered platform will support a wider range of form factors, despite many demoed features being mouse and voice-input focused.

Google previously named Lenovo, ASUS, Dell, and HP as hardware launch partners for Googlebooks, with an official launch anticipated later this year. The initiative is expected to roll out separately from Google's phone releases.

headline_marked: [[Google exempts sanctioned nations from Android developer verification]]
headline: Google exempts sanctioned nations from Android developer verification
summary: The policy means developers in these regions won't be able to verify, limiting their international app distribution. Users in these countries will also miss out on the program's enhanced security benefits.
details: Google's new Android developer verification system is set to roll out next month, blocking apps from unverified developers on most Android devices. To continue releasing software, even outside the Play Store, developers must provide ID and pay a small fee.

However, Google has confirmed an exemption for sanctioned nations, including Iran, Cuba, North Korea, and occupied areas of Ukraine. Devices in these regions will be excluded from verification checks, allowing local developers to distribute apps without verification.

Despite this local flexibility, Google has clarified that developers residing in sanctioned nations will not be permitted to complete the official verification process. This effectively prevents them from distributing their software internationally through verified channels.

Currently, a developer in a country like Cuba can distribute apps globally, but with the new policy, their unverified apps will only be easily installable in sanctioned countries. This creates a two-tiered system, linking Android app distribution capabilities to the US Treasury Department's sanctions list.

While an 'advanced flow' exists to bypass verification with several steps and a 24-hour wait, most users are unlikely to discover or utilize this option. Google states these changes are vital for combating scam apps, yet paradoxically, they introduce more app freedom within sanctioned nations.
